title: Deconstruct Constraints and Targets
subtitle: Extract the non-negotiable business rules before selecting any Azure service.
complexityDrivers: Number of regulatory frameworks in scope (HIPAA, PCI, GDPR)
Data residency constraints eliminating preferred region pairs
Multiple business units with conflicting SLA requirements
deliverables: Quantified RTO and RPO per application tier
Composite SLA calculation proving design meets availability target
Approved Azure region pair with data residency justification
Constraint register (inputs to all downstream steps)

subSteps.title: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
subSteps.question: How much data loss is acceptable?
subSteps.summary: RPO is the maximum tolerable age of data that can be lost on failure. It is measured backwards from the failure event and is primarily a business decision driven by a Business Impact Analysis, not a technical constraint.
keyPoints: Financial transaction databases often require near-zero RPO; internal HR records may tolerate 24-hour RPO
RPO directly determines which Azure replication mechanism is viable
HIPAA and PCI DSS impose maximum data loss windows — compliance can override business preference
Higher data change rates require shorter RPO windows due to more data generated per minute

serviceMapping.mechanism: Daily snapshot to Recovery Services Vault

subSteps.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
subSteps.question: How long can the system be completely offline?
subSteps.summary: RTO is the maximum tolerable duration of a service outage. Measured forward from the failure event — if the system fails at 3:00 PM and RTO is 2 hours, it must be operational by 5:00 PM. Set by the business through cost-of-downtime analysis.
keyPoints: The slowest dependency in the recovery chain sets the actual RTO floor — not the fastest component
Active-active architectures achieve < 1 minute RTO; cold standby may take hours
SLA penalty clauses create hard RTO floors — missing them triggers financial and legal consequences
Test RTO under realistic conditions, not just theoretical estimates

serviceMapping.services: Front Door + App Service (multi-region) + Cosmos DB multi-write
Traffic Manager + App Service + SQL Auto-Failover Group
DNS update + VM snapshots + Azure Backup restore

subSteps.title: Composite SLA
subSteps.question: Does the design mathematically meet the availability requirement?
subSteps.summary: A Composite SLA is the mathematical product of all component SLAs in a serial dependency chain. It is always lower than the weakest individual component. Understanding the serial vs. parallel formula is essential — stacking two 99.99% components in series produces 99.98%, doubling annual downtime.
keyPoints: Serial formula: SLA₁ × SLA₂ × SLA₃ — availability always decreases
Parallel (redundant) formula: 1 - ((1 - SLA₁) × (1 - SLA₂)) — availability increases
99.99% → 99.98% serial degradation doubles annual downtime from 52 min to 1 hr 45 min
Composite SLA calculation is a gating deliverable — if math cannot meet target, redesign first

subSteps.title: Data Residency
subSteps.question: Where must data physically exist?
subSteps.summary: Data residency is a legal mandate, not an optimization. It creates hard geographic boundaries that override architectural preferences and can force disaster recovery into a smaller region footprint than availability math would prefer.
keyPoints: GDPR: EU/EEA personal data cannot replicate to US regions without Standard Contractual Clauses
FedRAMP High: Azure Government regions only (USGov Virginia ↔ USGov Arizona pair)
HIPAA: No specific residency mandate but requires signed BAA with Microsoft
Document the constraint explicitly — it cascades into region pair selection in Steps 3 and 4

residencyTable.azureRegionPair: Germany West Central ↔ Germany North, or West Europe ↔ North Europe

title: Establish the Identity, Security, and Observability Boundary
subtitle: Define who owns what and how access is controlled before designing compute or network.
complexityDrivers: Number of management groups and subscription topology depth
Azure Policy initiative scope (built-in vs custom)
Hybrid identity (on-premises AD sync vs cloud-native)
Network perimeter model (Service Endpoints vs Private Link at scale)
Sentinel integration and custom analytic rules
deliverables: Management group and subscription topology diagram
Network perimeter decision: Private Link vs Service Endpoints
Microsoft Entra ID baseline (Conditional Access policies)
Azure Policy initiative assignment record
Central Log Analytics workspace + Sentinel workspace provisioned
Azure Activity Log routing to central workspace confirmed
criticalPathNote: This step gates IaC design and all downstream technical steps. At Tier 2 and Tier 3, rushing past an incomplete governance boundary produces technical debt that is expensive to remediate — Azure Policy scope changes and management group restructuring after resources are deployed require resource moves.

subSteps.title: Define the Isolation Layer
subSteps.question: What is the management group and subscription hierarchy?
subSteps.summary: The Azure resource hierarchy is your administrative boundary system. Management Groups contain Subscriptions, which contain Resource Groups, which contain resources. Design this top-down before creating any resources — restructuring after deployment is disruptive.
keyPoints: Each subscription is a blast radius boundary for quota, policy scope, and billing
Use subscription vending at Tier 2+ to eliminate manual provisioning bottlenecks
Assign RBAC at management group level using built-in roles before creating custom ones
Tag every subscription with environment, cost-center, owner, and workload-id at creation

subSteps.title: Design the Network Perimeter
subSteps.question: How does compute access PaaS services?
subSteps.summary: Production PaaS services should never be accessed over public endpoints. Private Endpoints inject PaaS service NICs into your VNet, eliminating public exposure. Service Endpoints are an acceptable middle-ground for lower-risk dev scenarios.
keyPoints: Private Link is the product; a Private Endpoint is the deployed resource instance
Private Endpoints require Private DNS Zone A records — budget for this at scale
20-service architecture may require 40+ private endpoint resources
Azure Policy can enforce 'deny public endpoint' on all PaaS services automatically

comparisonTable.whenToUse: Lower-risk scenarios; acceptable when exfiltration risk is low
All production; mandatory for regulated workloads

subSteps.title: Enforce Zero-Trust
subSteps.question: Are access decisions verified continuously, regardless of network location?
subSteps.summary: Zero-Trust assumes breach. Every access request — whether from inside or outside the corporate network — must be explicitly verified. Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access is the primary enforcement mechanism in Azure.
keyPoints: Verify explicitly: evaluate every access request against identity, device, location, and risk signals
Least privilege: time-bound access via PIM instead of standing Owner/Contributor assignments
Assume breach: design systems to limit blast radius when credentials are compromised
Start Conditional Access policies in report-only mode — validate before enforcement

conditionalAccessPolicies.control: Require Intune compliant or Hybrid Entra joined

subSteps.title: Azure Policy Guardrails
subSteps.question: What configuration standards are automatically enforced?
subSteps.summary: Azure Policy prevents non-compliant resources from being created rather than remediating them after the fact. Start with built-in initiatives; add custom policies for organization-specific requirements.
keyPoints: DeployIfNotExists effect automatically remediates non-compliant existing resources
Deny effect blocks resource creation — use carefully, as it blocks portal deployment too
Assign at management group level to cover all child subscriptions automatically
Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (formerly Azure Security Benchmark) is the baseline initiative

builtInInitiatives.name: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5
builtInInitiatives.purpose: US federal and highly regulated workloads

subSteps.title: Microsoft Sentinel Integration
subSteps.question: How are raw logs converted into actionable threat intelligence?
subSteps.summary: Microsoft Sentinel is the SIEM/SOAR layer above Log Analytics. It correlates signals across all data sources — Entra ID, Azure activity, network, endpoints — into unified threat detection and automated response.
keyPoints: Sentinel workspace and Log Analytics workspace are separate resources — Sentinel is layered on top of LAW
Data connectors determine what flows into Sentinel — enable Microsoft connectors first
Analytics rules detect threats; automation rules trigger SOAR responses
Sentinel pricing is per-GB analyzed — use commitment tiers above 100 GB/day
criticalConnectors: Microsoft Entra ID (sign-in logs, audit logs, provisioning logs)

subSteps.title: Control Plane Auditing
subSteps.question: Who changed what Azure infrastructure, and when?
subSteps.summary: Azure Activity Logs capture every resource creation, modification, deletion, RBAC change, and policy update at the subscription level. Route these to the central Log Analytics workspace via a Management Group-level Diagnostic Setting.
keyPoints: A single Diagnostic Setting at Management Group level covers all child subscriptions
Retention: 90 days hot in Log Analytics; 1+ year cold in Azure Storage for compliance
Activity Logs are free — the cost is only Log Analytics ingestion
Key Vault access logs are critical — every secret read is a potential security event

subSteps.title: Establish Observability
subSteps.question: Can you see what is happening across all layers in real time?
subSteps.summary: Observability is not a monitoring nicety — it is a security requirement. Zero-Trust requires continuous validation. You cannot detect anomalous credential use without sign-in log streaming, and you cannot detect data exfiltration without NSG Flow Logs.
keyPoints: Zero-Trust without observability is unenforced policy — you cannot validate what you cannot see
NSG Flow Logs + Traffic Analytics detect exfiltration over authorized ports to unauthorized destinations
Place central Log Analytics workspace in a dedicated management subscription with resource locks
Immutable audit trails are a regulatory requirement for PCI DSS, HIPAA, and FedRAMP

observabilityStack.captures: CPU, memory, disk, network — all resources

Cross-service correlation IDs, end-to-end request traces across microservices, AKS pods, and external dependencies. W3C TraceContext (traceparent header) must be propagated by all services — missing it silently breaks the trace graph.
Correlated threat signals across all layers
Service-specific events (SQL queries, Key Vault ops)

title: Map the Data Flow and Storage Tiers
subtitle: Data architecture dictates network and compute design — not the other way around.
complexityDrivers: Number of distinct data domains and their independence
Mixed data models in the same workload
Cross-region replication requirements from Step 1 residency constraints
Legacy data migration from on-premises
deliverables: Data classification matrix
Replication strategy per data store mapped to RPO targets
Split-brain prevention mechanism documented
Storage tier lifecycle policy designed
Data flow diagram (sources → processing → storage → consumers)

subSteps.title: Classify Data Structure
subSteps.question: What is the shape of the data?
subSteps.summary: Data classification drives service selection. Choosing a service before classifying data results in architectural mismatches — relational patterns in a document store, or document patterns in a relational store.

subSteps.title: Choose Replication Depth
subSteps.question: What replication mechanism satisfies the RPO from Step 1?
subSteps.summary: Replication strategy must flow from the RPO and data residency constraints established in Step 1. Selecting replication independently introduces risk of mismatch.

replicationOptions.mode: Daily snapshot to Recovery Services Vault

subSteps.title: Handle Split-Brain Scenarios
subSteps.question: What prevents both primary and replica from becoming write master simultaneously?
subSteps.summary: Split-brain occurs when both instances promote themselves to primary during a network partition, causing divergent writes that are expensive or impossible to reconcile.
keyPoints: SQL Auto-Failover Groups use quorum-based failover — set GracePeriodWithDataLossHours explicitly
Cosmos DB multi-write uses Last-Write-Wins (LWW) or custom conflict resolution functions
Redis geo-replication is active-passive only — active-active requires application-level logic
Design rule: there must always be exactly one write master for relational data during failover

subSteps.title: Storage Tier Selection
subSteps.question: Which access tier matches each dataset's usage pattern?
subSteps.summary: Blob storage cost is driven by tier selection. Over-provisioning cold data in Hot tier is the most common source of preventable Azure storage cost.

subSteps.title: Data Gravity and Movement Costs
subSteps.question: Where should compute live relative to its data?
subSteps.summary: Data gravity is the tendency for compute to cluster around large data stores. Moving large datasets is expensive and may be restricted by data residency rules. Place compute in the same region as its primary data store.

title: Design the Network Routing and Compute Abstraction
subtitle: Connect users to compute with the right traffic routing and scaling model.
complexityDrivers: Number of distinct entry points (public, private, on-premises)
Stateful vs stateless compute
Multi-region active-active
ExpressRoute provisioning lead time: 4–8 weeks
deliverables: Global routing decision (Front Door vs Traffic Manager) with justification
Compute platform selection per workload tier with scaling policy
Network topology diagram
Autoscaling configuration targets
Caching strategy per data access pattern
ExpressRoute or VPN Gateway circuit design (if hybrid)

subSteps.title: Select the Global Router
subSteps.question: Where does traffic enter the Azure network and how is it distributed?
subSteps.summary: The global routing layer determines where TLS terminates, where WAF rules are enforced, and how failover between regions is orchestrated. This decision must be made before network topology is finalized.

subSteps.title: Choose Compute Platform
subSteps.question: Which compute abstraction matches the workload's state, scale, and operational model?
subSteps.summary: Compute selection is driven by three axes: state (stateless vs stateful), scale pattern (event-driven vs sustained), and operational overhead tolerance.

computeOptions.whenToUse: Web apps, APIs; standard PaaS; Tier 1–2
Complex microservices, platform engineering layer, Tier 2–3

subSteps.title: Autoscaling Design
subSteps.question: How does the system respond to changes in demand without manual intervention?
subSteps.summary: Autoscaling prevents both over-provisioning (cost) and under-provisioning (performance degradation). Design scaling policy before deployment — retrofitting autoscale to a running system is error-prone.
keyPoints: Target 60–70% average CPU utilization with headroom for burst — not 10–20%
Set scale-in cooldown to 2× the longest request duration to prevent premature scale-in
AKS: Cluster Autoscaler (node level) + HPA (pod level) + KEDA (event-driven) work together
Use Pod Disruption Budgets to prevent scale-in from removing too many replicas simultaneously

subSteps.title: Caching Strategy
subSteps.question: What data can be served from cache instead of the primary store?
subSteps.summary: Caching reduces database load, decreases latency, and lowers egress costs. Each layer targets a different access pattern. The cache-aside pattern is the most common enterprise implementation.

cachingLayers.whatToCache: Session state, auth tokens, computed aggregates

subSteps.title: Hybrid Connectivity
subSteps.question: ExpressRoute or VPN Gateway — or both?
subSteps.summary: For workloads requiring on-premises integration, the connectivity model must be selected in Step 4 because ExpressRoute has a 4–8 week carrier provisioning lead time. Starting this decision late blocks the entire network topology.

comparisonTable.expressRoute: Not encrypted by default — add MACsec

title: Conduct a Blast Radius Failure Analysis
subtitle: Stress-test the design on paper by simulating total failures of individual components.
complexityDrivers: Number of distinct failure domains
Complexity of data failover chain
On-premises dependency on ExpressRoute
deliverables: Failure scenario matrix with expected behavior per component
RTO/RPO compliance confirmation per scenario
Single points of failure (SPOFs) identified and remediation plan
Chaos engineering test plan

subSteps.title: Simulate Region Loss
subSteps.question: If Region A vanishes at 2 AM with no warning, what happens to each component?
subSteps.summary: For each component, document: what fails, whether recovery is automatic, what manual action is required, and the RTO contribution. Identify every Single Point of Failure (SPOF).
spofPatterns: A session store (Redis) without geo-replication where loss logs users out
A single VPN Gateway with no ExpressRoute failover
An AKS cluster with Availability Zone spread disabled
A Key Vault without soft-delete and purge protection enabled

subSteps.title: Simulate Transient Network Drops
subSteps.question: The ExpressRoute circuit drops for 15 minutes. What breaks, what holds?
subSteps.summary: Transient network partitions are the most common real failure mode. BGP failover to VPN Gateway should be automatic — verify it is configured and tested.

keyChecks.question: Does VPN Gateway automatically take over?
keyChecks.badAnswer: No — requires manual route table change

keyChecks.question: Do applications retry on transient failures?
Does on-premises AD sync continue?
keyChecks.goodAnswer: No — but Entra ID caches for 1–4 hours

keyChecks.question: Do health probes alert before user impact?
keyChecks.badAnswer: No — first notice is user complaints

retryPattern.circuitBreaker: Open after 5 consecutive failures; half-open probe after 60 seconds

subSteps.title: Simulate Service-Level Degradation
subSteps.question: The database is up but responding 10× slower than normal. Is the system designed to degrade gracefully?
subSteps.summary: Partial failures are harder to detect than total outages and more common. Graceful degradation means the system returns a reduced-capability response rather than an error.

detectionMechanisms.tooling: Application Insights availability test + alert rule
Azure SQL Intelligent Insights + Query Performance Insight
App Insights dependency failure rate metric

title: Apply FinOps Optimizations
subtitle: Refine the final architecture for cost efficiency without sacrificing reliability or security.
complexityDrivers: Number of subscriptions requiring cost aggregation
Reserved Instance commitment duration decisions
FinOps maturity of the organization
deliverables: Right-sizing recommendation per compute resource
Reserved Instance / Savings Plan commitment recommendation
Storage lifecycle policy applied to all blob containers
Azure Cost Management budget + alert configuration
Cost allocation tag taxonomy enforced via Policy
FinOps maturity assessment

subSteps.title: Right-Size Compute Resources
subSteps.question: Are resources sized for actual utilization, not theoretical peak?
subSteps.summary: Over-provisioning is the most common Azure cost waste. Collect 30 days of utilization data before making sizing decisions. Target 60–70% average CPU, not 10–20%.

subSteps.title: Storage Lifecycle Management
subSteps.question: Is data automatically transitioned to cheaper tiers as it ages?
subSteps.summary: Application logs, diagnostic data, and backup exports accumulate silently in Hot tier. A lifecycle policy that moves data to Cool at 30 days and Archive at 90 days can reduce storage costs by 80–95% for inactive data.
keyPoints: 1 TB at Hot tier: ~$20/month. Same at Archive tier: ~$1/month — 95% reduction with a Lifecycle policy
Apply lifecycle policies to all storage accounts at deployment time, not retrospectively
Archive rehydration takes hours — document which data may need emergency retrieval

subSteps.title: Cost Allocation and Tagging
subSteps.question: Can every dollar of Azure spend be attributed to the right team and workload?
subSteps.summary: Cost Management analysis is only actionable if costs can be attributed. Tagging is the mechanism — enforce via Azure Policy DeployIfNotExists at resource group creation.

subSteps.title: Azure Cost Management Budgets
subSteps.question: Are there automated alerts before overspend occurs?
subSteps.summary: Budgets set the control threshold; alerts notify the right people before costs become a crisis. Configure before the workload goes live.

subSteps.title: FinOps Maturity Assessment
subSteps.question: What level of cost management discipline does this organization currently operate at?
subSteps.summary: The FinOps Foundation defines three maturity levels. Prescribing Run-level tooling to a Crawl organization creates overhead without delivering the cultural change needed for FinOps adoption.

maturityLevels.characteristics: Ad-hoc reviews, no tagging, no budgets
Monthly reviews, budgets per team, some RI purchases
maturityLevels.azureTooling: Budgets + anomaly detection + reserved instance management

maturityLevels.characteristics: Weekly optimization, full chargeback, automated rightsizing
maturityLevels.azureTooling: Azure Monitor + custom dashboards + automated Advisor

title: Establish the Operational Model
subtitle: Define how the architecture is deployed, changed, monitored, and recovered — by people, not just tools.
complexityDrivers: Number of teams owning different platform components
Regulatory change management requirements (CAB process)
GitOps maturity of the engineering team
Number of environments requiring promotion pipeline
deliverables: IaC repository structure with branching strategy
CI/CD pipeline design (environment promotion gates)
Deployment safety pattern selected
Runbook library
On-call rotation and escalation path
Post-incident review (PIR) process documented

subSteps.title: Infrastructure as Code Discipline
subSteps.question: Is all Azure infrastructure defined in version-controlled code?
subSteps.summary: Resources created through the Azure portal are configuration drift. All production resources must be defined in IaC. Bicep is the recommended choice for Azure-native deployments.

iacOptions.whenToUse: Legacy — prefer Bicep for new work

subSteps.title: Deployment Safety Patterns
subSteps.question: What is the blast radius of a bad deployment, and how quickly can it be reversed?
subSteps.summary: Production deployments are the highest-risk change operation. Safety patterns reduce the blast radius of a bad deployment and define the rollback path before anything goes wrong.

subSteps.title: Change Management and GitOps
subSteps.question: Can every infrastructure change be traced to a pull request with documented approval?
subSteps.summary: At Tier 3, production changes require documented approval. GitOps makes the PR history the audit trail — every change has an author, a reviewer, a Bicep what-if output, and a deployment record.
keyPoints: Bicep what-if output is a required PR artifact for infrastructure changes at Tier 2+
Security scans (Checkov / PSRule for Azure) run automatically in CI
Manual approval gate before production deployment — never fully automated for infrastructure
CAB integration at Tier 3: PR merge triggers CAB notification; production gate requires CAB approval record

subSteps.title: Incident Response Runbooks
subSteps.question: Can any on-call engineer resolve every failure mode identified in Step 5?
subSteps.summary: Every failure mode from the blast radius analysis must have a corresponding runbook. A runbook is a documented, tested procedure that any on-call engineer can follow under pressure without domain expertise.

minimumRunbooks.keySteps: Verify alert → confirm region status → trigger SQL failover → verify DNS → confirm traffic shift → notify
Point-in-time restore → validation queries → rollback decision criteria
Isolation → evidence preservation → escalation → regulatory notification timeline
Slot swap reversal / canary reduction / feature flag disable → post-mortem trigger

subSteps.title: Post-Incident Review (PIR) Process
subSteps.question: Does the team get systematically better after every significant incident?
subSteps.summary: A blameless PIR after every significant incident drives continuous improvement. Organizations that run blame-oriented post-mortems see recurring incidents because engineers avoid reporting near-misses.
